notes:
Deuteronomy 32:1–26: research notes

I was able to read three main sources: David Guzik (Enduring Word), Precept Austin, and verse pages on BibleHub and StudyLight. That last group includes Gill, Clarke, Ellicott, Poole, Benson, Barnes, the Pulpit Commentary and Keil & Delitzsch. I also used the NET Bible note on v. 8. **What I didn't find:** anything on the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran-site, or prosperity / word-of-faith / hyper-grace readings of this passage. So those views are left out, and the "differences between traditions" points are thin. Precept Austin's page only loaded for v. 1, so it barely appears for later verses.

**Overview**
- Guzik sees the whole song as prophecy about Israel's future. In his reading, the deep corruption it describes came after Moses and Joshua, not in their day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Ellicott's notes say the song looks ahead to conditions that came long after Moses. If Moses could foresee Israel turning away, he says, a song is the best possible way to warn them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/32-1.htm
- The Layman's Bible Commentary says the song follows the pattern of a "covenant lawsuit," a formal charge against people who broke the covenant, though loosely. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/deuteronomy-32.html

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Moses asks all creation to listen. He links this to Moses calling heaven and earth as witnesses earlier (Deut 30:19; 31:28) and says it is not to a supposed divine council. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (via BibleHub) says the solemn appeal shows two things: the message matters to the whole world, and the people were dull, less likely to listen than heaven and earth themselves. Gill mentions Gaon's view (reported by Aben Ezra) that "heavens" means angels and "earth" means people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/32-1.htm
- Precept Austin, citing Matthew Henry and Spurgeon: heaven and earth are called as witnesses against people who are slow to hear. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-32-commentary

**v. 2**
- Guzik: Moses prays that his teaching will nourish Israel the way rain and dew nourish plants, and he links this to Isaiah 55:10–11. He also quotes Spurgeon, who saw here a picture of good preaching that soaks in like a gentle shower. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Wiersbe (via Precept Austin): God's Word works like rain, doing its purpose even when we can't see the results. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-32-commentary

**v. 3**
- Constable: God is the subject of the song. His "name" stands for his character as he has revealed it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-32.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik: the praise is for who God is (the Rock, righteous, upright) and for what he does (his work is perfect, his ways are just). He quotes Clarke: rocks were places of safety in those lands, so the title points to God's protection. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Wiersbe (via Precept Austin): "the Rock" is the key image for God in the song. It speaks of his stability and dependability. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-32-commentary
- James Smith (via Precept Austin) applies "the Rock" to Christ, the "Perfect Worker" who finishes what he starts (Phil 1:6). https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-32-commentary

**v. 5**
- Guzik: Moses speaks as a witness against a future rebellious Israel. He quotes Trapp's line that preachers should speak against sin as freely as people commit it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary uses the "spot" image: sin stains like spots on the face, and grace restores God's likeness in his children. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/32-8.html

**v. 6**
- Guzik: Israel acted as though they were not God's children (v. 5), yet Moses still appeals to God as their Father. Rebelling against the God who made them was foolish. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Precept Austin: Israel's folly was choosing to provoke God by unfaithfulness. In the Bible, being a "fool" goes with unbelief. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-32-commentary

**v. 7**
- Guzik: Moses lists God's past goodness to make Israel feel their sin more deeply, and to remind them of the grace they could come back to. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- John Maxwell (Preacher's Commentary, via Precept Austin): the call to "remember" comes sixteen times in Deuteronomy, from 4:10 to here. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-32-commentary

**v. 8: the main textual and interpretive debate**
- **Two manuscript readings.** BibleHub notes that the Masoretic Text, the standard Hebrew text, reads "sons of Israel." A Dead Sea Scroll fragment (4QDeutʲ) and the Greek Septuagint have wording meaning "sons of God" or "angels of God." Some suggest scribes changed the wording to avoid any hint of many gods. https://biblehub.com/q/how_does_deut._32_8_align_with_ancient_texts.htm
- **Translations split.** KJV, NKJV, NASB, NIV and CSB say "sons/children/people of Israel." ESV, RSV and NRSV have "sons of God" or "the gods"; NLT has his "heavenly court"; NET, "the heavenly assembly." Brenton's Septuagint says "angels of God." The Catholic Douay-Rheims follows the Latin Vulgate and has "children of Israel," while the Catholic New American Bible has "the divine beings." https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/32-8.htm
- **Traditional "sons of Israel" reading.** Guzik follows it and quotes Clarke: God set aside twelve portions for Jacob's sons when he divided the earth. He also quotes Kalland: God rules over who gets which land in every generation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- BibleHub mentions a related idea: the 70 people of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:27) match the nations listed in Genesis 10. https://biblehub.com/study/deuteronomy/32-8.htm
- **"Heavenly beings" reading.** A Desiring God (Baptist) article reads the verse in light of the Tower of Babel. On that reading, the sons of God would seem to be heavenly beings assigned by God to the various nations of mankind, while Israel is the Lord's own portion. It ties this to Psalm 82. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-divine-council
- BibleHub's commentary page links the same idea to the angelic "princes" of Persia and Greece in Daniel 10. https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/32-8.htm
- **NET Bible note:** "Most High" (Elyon) is a short form of El Elyon. The note says Elyon is linked with the nations in general, while in v. 9 the LORD (Yahweh) is linked specifically with Israel. https://bible.org/netbible/deu32_notes.htm
- **Older Protestant readings:** Gill and Clarke place the division of the earth in the days of Noah's sons and Peleg (Gen 10:25). Clarke, citing Kennicott, thinks it may have been done by lot (Acts 17:26). https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brl/deuteronomy/32-8.html
- The Pulpit/Lange material quotes Calvin: God arranged the whole world with the good of his chosen people in mind. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/32-8.html
- Matthew Henry sees the early setting apart of Canaan as a picture of the heavenly inheritance, planned in advance. https://biblehub.com/sermons/deuteronomy/32-8.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik quotes Clarke: just as holy people take God as their portion, God takes them as his. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Guzik also quotes Thompson's outline of the section: Israel chosen (vv. 8–9), rescued in the Exodus (vv. 10–12), and given Canaan (vv. 13–14). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- NET note: the contrast is between Elyon and the nations in v. 8 and Yahweh's special bond with Israel here. https://bible.org/netbible/deu32_notes.htm

**v. 10**
- Guzik quotes Kalland: "apple of his eye" renders the Hebrew "little man of his eye," meaning the pupil, something deeply cherished. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

**v. 11**
- Guzik: God cares for Israel as an eagle protects its young, and he links this to Exodus 19:4. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Precept Austin's devotional section pictures God as a mother eagle her young can trust while they learn to fly. Wiersbe likens Israel to young eagles that must leave the nest. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-32-commentary

**v. 12**
- Guzik: all this was the gift of the LORD alone, with no foreign god involved. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

**v. 13**
- Guzik quotes Merrill: "ride on the heights" (literally "ride the backs") suggests power and victory (Hab 3:19). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- James Smith (via Precept Austin) treats the honey and oil from the rock as pictures of Christ's grace and the Holy Spirit's power. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-32-commentary

**v. 14**
- Guzik: God's provision brought Israel to Bashan, east of the Jordan, which became Israel's land. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

**v. 15**
- Guzik: "Jeshurun" is a name for Israel meaning "the upright one" (Isa 44:2). He stresses the shocking contrast between God's blessings (vv. 7–14) and Israel's rebellion (vv. 15–18). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Through Thompson, Guzik cites Luther's comment that 'A full stomach does not promote piety'. This is the only Lutheran voice I found. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: prosperity is a harder test than hardship. He quotes Kalland: the only other use of "kicked" is 1 Samuel 2:29, where it means "scorn." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Keil & Delitzsch see vv. 16–18 as an expansion of v. 15. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/32-17.htm

**v. 16**
- Guzik: turning to foreign gods was treating God with scorn. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

**v. 17: what were the "demons"?**
- **The word.** The Pulpit Commentary says the Hebrew *shedim* appears only here and in Psalm 106:37, and is linked to a verb meaning "to rule," so basically "lords." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/32-17.htm
- Clarke (labelled Arminian/Methodist) notes that the Septuagint, Vulgate and others translate it "demons/devils." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/32-17.html
- Barnes translates it "destroyers," pointing to the pagan belief that the gods were hostile and had to be appeased with human suffering. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/asv/deuteronomy/32-17.html
- **Real spirits behind the idols.** Guzik (Pentecostal-leaning Calvary Chapel): idol worship honoured real demonic spirits, not imaginary beings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Poole: Moses removes the mask and shows the so-called gods were really devils. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/32-17.htm
- Benson takes a similar line: whatever the people intended, their sacrifices actually went to devils. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/32-17.html
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) goes further: demons may actually be attached to idols, so sincerity in a false religion does not save. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/32-17.html
- **A different emphasis (Barnes).** On 1 Corinthians 10:20, Barnes argues pagans did not knowingly worship "devils" in the popular sense, because they didn't know such beings existed. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/1-corinthians/10-20.html
- **New Testament use.** Ellicott (labelled Anglican) and BibleHub note that Paul repeats this wording in 1 Corinthians 10:20. Ellicott's printed reference says 11:20, which looks like a misprint. https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/32-17.htm
- Calvin, on 1 Corinthians 10:20, links the verse to Deuteronomy 32:17 via the Septuagint's word "demons." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/10-20.html
- **"Newly arrived gods."** Ellicott: literally "that came from close at hand." The Pulpit Commentary says the word means "near" in time, so gods recently invented. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/32-17.htm
- **A tradition-specific application.** Gill (labelled Calvinist/Baptist) applies the verse to later Jewish sacrifices offered after God meant them to stop. He also aims it at "Pagans and Papists," a polemic of his 18th-century setting. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/32-17.html

**v. 18**
- James Smith (via Precept Austin): "the Rock who brought you forth" shows that Christ gives life. Being a Christian means being born of God, not just joining a system (John 3:3). https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-32-commentary
- Wiersbe: Moses reminds them not to forget their beginning. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-32-commentary

**v. 19**
- Clarke links the promise in v. 21 to the rejection of the Jews threatened here. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/deuteronomy/32-21.html

**v. 20**
- Guzik: hiding his face is the opposite of the priestly blessing, "the LORD make his face shine upon you" (Num 6:25). "Children of unfaithfulness" shows they didn't truly trust God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: every unbeliever will be shut out of the gospel's blessing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

**v. 21: Paul's use in Romans 10:19**
- Clarke calls the verse a very pointed promise of the calling of the Gentiles, in consequence of the rejection of the Jews, and notes Paul applies it this way. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/deuteronomy/32-21.html
- Precept Austin (on Romans): Gentiles would be saved and Israel made jealous, as Moses foretold. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_1019-21
- Barnes: in its original setting the verse is about the Jews' idolatry. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/romans/10-19.html
- Guzik's summary: the song ends with hope for Israel and for the Gentiles, fulfilled in Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

**v. 22**
- Guzik quotes Clarke: "burns to the depths of Sheol" means complete destruction. The land and its crops would be lost, and the "foundations of the mountains" means their strongest forts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

**v. 23**
- Guzik: the poetic repetition shows how intense the judgment is. He quotes Clarke that "arrows" stands for God's judgments in general (Job 6:4; Ps 38:2). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

**v. 24**
- Guzik: hunger and disease would wear God's people down. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

**v. 25**
- Guzik quotes Merrill: covenant rebellion would bring bitter results Israel didn't seem to see coming. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/

**v. 26** (the thought finishes in v. 27)
- Guzik: God would hold back from wiping out Israel's memory because the enemy nations would boast that they had done it, not the LORD. In his overview, judgment is meant to discipline and purify, not destroy completely. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-32/
- Precept Austin's sermon outline reads the verse as God wanting to preserve his people, not erase their name. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-32-commentary
